anatomy.heart.overview: Sits in the center of the chest, near the lungs. It has four hollow chambers surrounded by muscle and other heart tissue.
anatomy.heart.function: Pumps blood through the lungs and the body.

anatomy.heart.chambers.overview: The heart has two atria and two ventricles.
anatomy.heart.chambers.function: Atria receive blood; ventricles pump it onward.

anatomy.heart.septum.overview: A wall separates the right and left sides of the heart.
anatomy.heart.septum.function: The interventricular portion separates the ventricles.

anatomy.heart.atrium.right.overview: The right atrium is one of the upper chambers.
anatomy.heart.atrium.right.function: Receives blood returning from the body.

anatomy.heart.atrium.left.overview: The left atrium is one of the upper chambers.
anatomy.heart.atrium.left.function: Receives blood returning from the lungs.

anatomy.heart.ventricle.right.overview: The right ventricle is a lower chamber.
anatomy.heart.ventricle.right.function: Pumps blood toward the lungs through the pulmonary valve.

anatomy.heart.ventricle.left.overview: The left ventricle is a lower chamber.
anatomy.heart.ventricle.left.function: Pumps blood through the aortic valve toward the body.

anatomy.heart.valves.overview: Four valves control forward flow through the heart.
anatomy.heart.valves.function: Their leaflets open and close to limit backward flow.

anatomy.heart.valve.tricuspid.overview: Between the right atrium and right ventricle.

anatomy.heart.valve.pulmonary.overview: Between the right ventricle and pulmonary artery.

anatomy.heart.valve.mitral.overview: Between the left atrium and left ventricle.

anatomy.heart.valve.aortic.overview: Between the left ventricle and aorta.

anatomy.lungs.overview: The main organs of the respiratory system, one on each side of the heart inside the chest cavity.
anatomy.lungs.function: Exchange oxygen and carbon dioxide between air and blood.

anatomy.lung.left.overview: The left lung has two lobes. It is slightly smaller than the right lung because the heart takes up some space on the left side.

anatomy.lung.right.overview: The right lung has three lobes.

anatomy.aorta.overview: The main artery of the body, leaving the left ventricle through the aortic valve.
anatomy.aorta.function: Carries oxygen-rich blood from the heart to the rest of the body.

anatomy.coronary.left.overview: One of the two coronary arteries that branch from the aorta and run over the surface of the heart.
anatomy.coronary.left.function: Supplies oxygen-rich blood to the heart muscle.

anatomy.coronary.right.overview: One of the two coronary arteries that branch from the aorta and run over the surface of the heart.
anatomy.coronary.right.function: Supplies oxygen-rich blood to the heart muscle.

anatomy.vena-cava.superior.overview: One of the two venae cavae, the large veins through which blood returns to the heart.
anatomy.vena-cava.superior.function: Returns oxygen-poor blood from the body to the right atrium.

anatomy.vena-cava.inferior.overview: One of the two venae cavae, the large veins through which blood returns to the heart.
anatomy.vena-cava.inferior.function: Returns oxygen-poor blood from the body to the right atrium.

anatomy.pulmonary-veins.overview: Veins running from the lungs back to the heart.
anatomy.pulmonary-veins.function: Return oxygen-rich blood from the lungs to the left atrium.

anatomy.trachea.overview: The windpipe: the airway that leads from the larynx (voice box) to the bronchi. In the chest it divides into the right and left primary bronchi.
anatomy.trachea.function: Carries air between the larynx and the bronchi, which lead to the lungs.

anatomy.bronchi.overview: The right and left primary bronchi branch from the trachea into smaller and smaller airways inside the lungs.
anatomy.bronchi.function: Conduct air between the trachea and the tiny air sacs of the lungs.

anatomy.liver.overview: The largest gland in the body, lying mainly in the upper right abdomen just beneath the diaphragm.
anatomy.liver.function: Makes bile and processes the nutrient-rich blood that arrives from the digestive tract through the hepatic portal vein.

anatomy.gallbladder.overview: A pear-shaped sac attached to the underside of the liver.
anatomy.gallbladder.function: Stores bile between meals and squeezes it through the bile ducts into the small intestine when you eat.

anatomy.bile-duct.common.overview: Part of the duct system that carries bile toward the small intestine.
anatomy.bile-duct.common.function: Delivers bile, which helps digest fats.

anatomy.pancreas.overview: One of the solid organs of the digestive system. Its digestive juice reaches the small intestine through small tubes called ducts.
anatomy.pancreas.function: Releases digestive enzymes into the small intestine and the hormones insulin and glucagon into the blood.

anatomy.portal-vein.overview: The hepatic portal vein leads to the liver.
anatomy.portal-vein.function: Carries nutrient-rich blood from the digestive tract to the liver.

anatomy.small-intestine.overview: A long tube divided into three parts: the duodenum, jejunum and ileum.
anatomy.small-intestine.function: Finishes digesting food and absorbs its nutrients.

anatomy.colon.overview: The main part of the large intestine, which also includes the rectum and anal canal.
anatomy.colon.function: Absorbs water and electrolytes and moves waste toward the rectum for elimination.

anatomy.appendix.overview: A finger-shaped pouch attached to the cecum, the first part of the large intestine.
anatomy.appendix.function: Part of the large intestine. Inflammation of the appendix is called appendicitis.

anatomy.spleen.overview: The largest lymphatic organ, in the upper left abdomen just beneath the diaphragm and behind the stomach.
anatomy.spleen.function: Filters blood. Its lymphocytes react to pathogens carried in the blood.

anatomy.thymus.overview: A lymphatic organ behind the sternum. It is relatively large in children and shrinks after puberty.
anatomy.thymus.function: Processes and matures special lymphocytes called T cells.

anatomy.kidneys.overview: Two bean-shaped organs, each about the size of a fist, just below the rib cage on each side of the spine.
anatomy.kidneys.function: Filter wastes and extra water from the blood to make urine, and make hormones that help control blood pressure.

anatomy.kidney.left.overview: Lies against the back wall of the abdomen, usually slightly higher than the right kidney.

anatomy.kidney.right.overview: Usually sits slightly lower than the left kidney because the liver displaces it downward.

anatomy.bladder.overview: Located in the pelvic cavity, behind the pubic symphysis. Its size and shape change with the amount of urine it holds.
anatomy.bladder.function: A temporary storage reservoir for urine.

anatomy.ureters.overview: Two small tubes, each about 25 cm long, that descend along the back wall of the abdomen.
anatomy.ureters.function: Carry urine from the kidneys to the bladder.

anatomy.uterus.overview: A muscular organ. Before a first pregnancy it is about the size and shape of a pear.
anatomy.uterus.function: Receives a fertilized egg and provides the environment for a developing fetus.

anatomy.ovaries.overview: Two almond-sized organs, one on each side of the uterus in the side walls of the pelvic cavity.
anatomy.ovaries.function: Develop egg cells and secrete hormones such as estrogen.

anatomy.prostate.overview: A gland that sits below the bladder and surrounds the urethra at the bladder's neck.
anatomy.prostate.function: An accessory gland whose secretions enter the urethra and form part of semen.

anatomy.brain.overview: Divided into the cerebrum, diencephalon, brain stem and cerebellum. With the spinal cord it forms the central nervous system.
anatomy.brain.function: The body's control center. It controls thoughts, memory, speech and movement, and regulates the function of many organs.

anatomy.cerebellum.overview: The second largest part of the brain, below the occipital lobes of the cerebrum. The supplied cerebellum is split into several source parts.
anatomy.cerebellum.function: Processes input from other areas of the brain, the spinal cord and sensory receptors to time coordinated, smooth movements.

anatomy.brainstem.overview: The region between the diencephalon and the spinal cord, made of three parts: the midbrain, pons and medulla oblongata.
anatomy.brainstem.function: Links the brain and spinal cord. All the sensory and motor nerve fibers connecting them pass through the medulla.

anatomy.thalamus.overview: Two oval masses of gray matter making up about 80 percent of the diencephalon, which the cerebral hemispheres nearly surround.
anatomy.thalamus.function: Relays sensory impulses, except for smell, to the cerebral cortex.

anatomy.hypothalamus.overview: A small region of the diencephalon below the thalamus.
anatomy.hypothalamus.function: Plays a key role in maintaining homeostasis because it regulates many visceral activities.

anatomy.corpus-callosum.overview: An arching band of white fibers joining the two cerebral hemispheres.
anatomy.corpus-callosum.function: Provides a communication pathway between the two halves of the cerebrum.

anatomy.eyes.overview: Light passes through the cornea, enters through the pupil, then passes through the lens to the retina at the back of the eye.
anatomy.eyes.function: The parts of the eye work together so you can see: they focus light and turn it into signals the brain makes into images.

anatomy.cornea.overview: The clear, dome-shaped front layer of the eye.
anatomy.cornea.function: Bends light to help the eye focus.

anatomy.iris.overview: The colored part of the eye, around an opening called the pupil.
anatomy.iris.function: Controls how much light the pupil lets in.

anatomy.lens.overview: A clear inner part of the eye. Light passes through it after entering through the pupil.
anatomy.lens.function: Works together with the cornea to focus light correctly on the retina.

anatomy.retina.overview: A light-sensitive layer of tissue at the back of the eye.
anatomy.retina.function: Special cells called photoreceptors turn light into electrical signals, which travel through the optic nerve to the brain.

anatomy.macula.overview: Part of the retina, the light-sensitive tissue at the back of the eye.

anatomy.optic-nerves.overview: Each optic nerve leaves the back of an eye.
anatomy.optic-nerves.function: Carries electrical signals from the retina to the brain.

anatomy.knee.overview: The joint where the end of the thigh bone (femur) meets the top of the shin bone (tibia). It is made up of bone, cartilage, ligaments and fluid.
anatomy.knee.function: Four main ligaments hold the joint together: the two cruciate ligaments connect the thigh bone and shin bone, and the two collateral ligaments run along its sides. Muscles and tendons help the joint move.

anatomy.femur.overview: The thigh bone. Its lower end meets the top of the shin bone at the knee joint.
anatomy.femur.function: Forms the upper part of the knee joint.

anatomy.tibia.overview: The shin bone. Its top meets the end of the thigh bone at the knee joint.
anatomy.tibia.function: Forms the lower part of the knee joint. The cruciate ligaments keep it from sliding forward or backward against the thigh bone.

anatomy.knee-cartilage.overview: Articular cartilage covers the ends of the bones where they meet in a freely movable joint. The supplied cartilage covers the lower end of the femur.
anatomy.knee-cartilage.function: Covers the bone ends inside the joint. In osteoarthritis this cartilage breaks down.

anatomy.meniscus.overview: A C-shaped piece of tough but flexible cartilage in the knee joint. Each knee has two.
anatomy.meniscus.function: Cushions the bones of the knee like a shock absorber, helps distribute weight to the cartilage and helps stabilize the joint.

anatomy.acl.overview: The anterior cruciate ligament, in the middle of the knee: one of the two cruciate ligaments, which connect the thigh bone and shin bone.
anatomy.acl.function: Prevents the shin bone from sliding out in front of the thigh bone.

anatomy.pcl.overview: The posterior cruciate ligament, one of the four main knee ligaments. It works opposite to the ACL.
anatomy.pcl.function: Prevents the shin bone from sliding backward under the thigh bone.

anatomy.mcl.overview: The medial collateral ligament, which runs along the inside of the knee.
anatomy.mcl.function: Prevents the knee from bending inward.

anatomy.lcl.overview: The lateral collateral ligament, which runs along the outside of the knee from the thigh bone to the head of the fibula.
anatomy.lcl.function: Prevents the knee from bending outward.

anatomy.pulmonary-arteries.overview: The pulmonary trunk leaves the right ventricle through the pulmonary valve. The supplied parts include the left and right pulmonary arteries.
anatomy.pulmonary-arteries.function: Carry oxygen-poor blood from the heart to the lungs.

anatomy.coronary-sinus.overview: A channel into which most of the cardiac veins drain. It opens into the right atrium.
anatomy.coronary-sinus.function: Returns blood from the cardiac veins to the right atrium.

anatomy.cardiac-veins.function: Most of them drain into the coronary sinus, which opens into the right atrium.

anatomy.aorta.ascending.overview: The first of the aorta's three portions: ascending aorta, aortic arch and descending aorta.
anatomy.aorta.ascending.function: The coronary arteries are the only vessels that branch from it.

anatomy.aorta.arch.overview: The middle of the aorta's three portions, between the ascending and descending aorta.
anatomy.aorta.arch.function: The brachiocephalic, left common carotid and left subclavian arteries branch from it.

anatomy.aorta.descending.overview: The last of the aorta's three portions, continuing down from the aortic arch.
anatomy.aorta.descending.function: In the abdomen, the celiac, superior mesenteric, renal and inferior mesenteric arteries branch from it to supply the abdominal organs.

anatomy.aortic-arch-branches.overview: The brachiocephalic, left common carotid and left subclavian arteries, which branch from the aortic arch.
anatomy.aortic-arch-branches.function: Carry blood from the aortic arch. The subclavian arteries supply the upper limbs.

anatomy.celiac-trunk.overview: An artery branching from the abdominal aorta.
anatomy.celiac-trunk.function: One of the arteries that supply the abdominal organs.

anatomy.mesenteric-artery.superior.overview: An artery branching from the abdominal aorta.
anatomy.mesenteric-artery.superior.function: One of the arteries that supply the abdominal organs.

anatomy.mesenteric-artery.inferior.overview: An artery branching from the abdominal aorta.
anatomy.mesenteric-artery.inferior.function: One of the arteries that supply the abdominal organs.

anatomy.renal-arteries.overview: Arteries branching from the abdominal aorta. Each enters a kidney at its hilum.
anatomy.renal-arteries.function: Bring blood to the kidneys to be filtered.

anatomy.renal-veins.overview: Veins that leave each kidney at its hilum.
anatomy.renal-veins.function: Carry blood away from the kidneys.

anatomy.larynx.overview: The larynx is formed by nine cartilages connected by muscles and ligaments. The thyroid cartilage is the Adam's apple.
anatomy.larynx.function: Produces sound: its vocal cords close together and vibrate as air from the lungs passes between them.

anatomy.epiglottis.overview: One of the cartilages of the larynx.
anatomy.epiglottis.function: Acts like a trap door to keep food and other particles from entering the larynx.

anatomy.tracheal-cartilage.overview: Hyaline cartilage in the wall of the trachea, the main airway to the lungs.
anatomy.tracheal-cartilage.function: Supports the trachea and keeps it from collapsing.

anatomy.lung.right.lobes.overview: The right lung is shorter and broader than the left and has a greater volume. It is divided into three lobes.
anatomy.lung.right.lobes.function: Each lobe is supplied by one of the secondary bronchi.

anatomy.lung.left.lobes.overview: The left lung is longer and narrower than the right lung. It has two lobes.
anatomy.lung.left.lobes.function: Each lobe is supplied by one of the secondary bronchi.

anatomy.lung-hilum.overview: The hilum, or root, on the medial side of each lung.
anatomy.lung-hilum.function: The only point of attachment for each lung.

anatomy.kidney-capsule.overview: A tough, fibrous connective tissue capsule that closely envelops each kidney.
anatomy.kidney-capsule.function: Supports the soft tissue inside the kidney.

anatomy.renal-cortex.overview: The outer, reddish region of the kidney, next to the capsule.

anatomy.renal-medulla.overview: A darker reddish-brown region surrounded by the renal cortex. It consists of a series of renal pyramids.
anatomy.renal-medulla.function: Its pyramids contain straight tubular structures and blood vessels.

anatomy.renal-pyramids.overview: The pyramids of the renal medulla. Their wide bases lie next to the cortex and their pointed ends, the renal papillae, face the center of the kidney.
anatomy.renal-pyramids.function: They appear striated because they contain straight tubular structures and blood vessels.

anatomy.renal-papillae.overview: The pointed ends of the renal pyramids, directed toward the center of the kidney.
anatomy.renal-papillae.function: Each is surrounded by a minor calyx that collects urine from its pyramid.

anatomy.minor-calyces.overview: Cuplike projections of the renal pelvis. A minor calyx surrounds the renal papillae of each pyramid.
anatomy.minor-calyces.function: Collect urine from each pyramid. Several minor calyces converge to form a major calyx.

anatomy.major-calyces.overview: Formed where several minor calyces converge.
anatomy.major-calyces.function: Part of the cuplike edge of the renal pelvis, which collects urine.

anatomy.renal-pelvis.overview: A large cavity in the central region of the kidney, continuous with the ureter.
anatomy.renal-pelvis.function: Collects the urine as it is produced.

anatomy.kidney-hilum.overview: An indentation on the medial side of each bean-shaped kidney.
anatomy.kidney-hilum.function: Where the renal artery enters the kidney and the ureter and renal vein leave it.

anatomy.duodenum.overview: The first part of the small intestine.
anatomy.duodenum.function: Part of the small intestine, which digests food and absorbs its nutrients.

anatomy.jejunum.overview: The middle of the three parts of the small intestine: duodenum, jejunum and ileum.
anatomy.jejunum.function: Part of the small intestine, which digests food and absorbs its nutrients.

anatomy.ileum.overview: The last of the three parts of the small intestine. It enters the large intestine at the ileocecal junction.
anatomy.ileum.function: Part of the small intestine, which digests food and absorbs its nutrients.

anatomy.ileocecal-valve.overview: Where the small intestine empties into the large intestine.
anatomy.ileocecal-valve.function: Marks the end of the small intestine.

anatomy.cecum.overview: Part of the large intestine, which includes the appendix, cecum, colon and rectum. The appendix is attached to it.
anatomy.cecum.function: Part of the large intestine, which absorbs water and moves waste toward the rectum.

anatomy.sigmoid-colon.overview: The lower part of the colon. The rectum continues from it.
anatomy.sigmoid-colon.function: Part of the colon, which absorbs water and moves waste toward the rectum.

anatomy.rectum.overview: The end of the large intestine. It continues from the sigmoid colon to the anal canal and has a thick muscular layer.
anatomy.rectum.function: Receives stool moved along from the colon by muscle contractions (peristalsis).

anatomy.liver-lobes.overview: On the surface, the liver is divided into two major lobes and two smaller lobes.
anatomy.liver-lobes.function: Together they make up the liver, which makes bile and processes nutrient-rich blood from the digestive tract.

anatomy.cystic-duct.overview: The duct that attaches the gallbladder to the underside of the liver.
anatomy.cystic-duct.function: Attaches the gallbladder to the liver.

anatomy.fallopian-tubes.overview: The two uterine tubes, also called Fallopian tubes or oviducts.
anatomy.fallopian-tubes.function: Fertilization usually occurs in a Fallopian tube, because an egg cell is fertile for only 24 to 48 hours.

anatomy.tube-infundibulum.overview: The funnel-shaped end of each tube near the ovary, surrounded by fingerlike extensions called fimbriae.
anatomy.tube-infundibulum.function: At ovulation the fimbriae become more active and create currents that help draw the egg cell into the tube.

anatomy.cervix.overview: The lower, narrow end of the uterus. It projects into the vagina at nearly a right angle.
anatomy.cervix.function: Connects the uterus to the vagina.

anatomy.vagina.overview: A fibromuscular tube, about 10 cm long, that extends from the cervix of the uterus to the outside.
anatomy.vagina.function: Connects the cervix to the outside of the body. It is also called the birth canal.

anatomy.lymph-node.overview: A sample lymph node. A typical node is surrounded by a connective tissue capsule and divided into compartments called lymph nodules.
anatomy.lymph-node.function: Lymph nodes lie along the lymphatic pathways and filter lymph before it returns to the blood.

anatomy.quadriceps-tendon.overview: The tendon of the quadriceps femoris muscle group, at the knee.
anatomy.quadriceps-tendon.function: The quadriceps femoris muscle group straightens the leg at the knee.

anatomy.pupil.overview: An opening through which light enters the eye.
anatomy.pupil.function: Lets light into the eye; the iris controls how much.

anatomy.ciliary-body.overview: One of the three parts of the uvea, with the iris and the choroid.

anatomy.choroid.overview: One of the three parts of the uvea, at the back of the eye.
anatomy.choroid.function: A layer of connective tissue and blood vessels between the retina and the sclera.

anatomy.vitreous.overview: The vitreous, a gel-like fluid that fills the eye.
anatomy.vitreous.function: Fills the eye. With age, tiny strands in it can stick together and cast shadows on the retina, seen as floaters.

anatomy.compact-bone.overview: Compact bone tissue, supplied here for the pubis, ilium and ischium of the pelvis.
anatomy.compact-bone.function: Made of closely packed osteons (haversian systems) that form what appears to be a solid mass.

anatomy.spongy-bone.overview: Spongy bone, made of plates (trabeculae) and bars of bone next to small, irregular cavities that contain red bone marrow. Supplied here for the pubis, ilium and ischium of the pelvis.
anatomy.spongy-bone.function: Its trabeculae follow the lines of stress and can realign if the direction of stress changes.

anatomy.skin.overview: The body's largest organ, covering the entire outside of the body. It is about 2 mm thick. Its outer layer, the epidermis, is tough and protective; the dermis beneath it contains nerve endings, sweat glands, oil glands and hair follicles.
anatomy.skin.function: Forms a protective barrier against pathogens and injury. It also helps regulate body temperature, gathers sensory information and stores water, fat and vitamin D.

anatomy.sclera.overview: The white layer of the eye.
anatomy.sclera.function: Covers most of the outside of the eyeball.

anatomy.conjunctiva.overview: A membrane that lines the inner surface of the eyelids and also covers the front part of the eye.
anatomy.conjunctiva.function: Lines and covers the front of the eye. Its inflammation is called conjunctivitis.

anatomy.optic-chiasm.overview: The place in the brain where some of the optic nerve fibers from one eye cross fibers from the other eye.
anatomy.optic-chiasm.function: Where optic nerve fibers from the two eyes partly cross on their way into the brain.

anatomy.olfactory-bulbs.overview: Two rounded masses of nerve tissue on the bottom side of the brain, one above each nasal cavity.
anatomy.olfactory-bulbs.function: Involved in the sense of smell: they receive information about smells from the nose and send it to the brain through the olfactory tracts.

anatomy.pineal-gland.overview: A small gland in the midline of the brain, between the two cerebral hemispheres, attached by a stalk to the back wall of the third ventricle. Also called the pineal body.
anatomy.pineal-gland.function: Produces melatonin, which regulates the body's daily (circadian) rhythm.

anatomy.brain-ventricles.overview: Fluid-filled cavities in the brain: the parts of each lateral ventricle, the third and fourth ventricles, and the cerebral aqueduct that connects the third ventricle to the fourth.
anatomy.brain-ventricles.function: Tissue called the choroid plexus in the ventricles makes cerebrospinal fluid, which flows in and around the hollow spaces of the brain and spinal cord.

anatomy.dura-mater.overview: The tough outer layer of the meninges, the three thin layers that cover and protect the brain and spinal cord. In these models, dura mater is supplied only with the nerves of each eye.
anatomy.dura-mater.function: Covers and protects the brain and spinal cord; it is the meningeal layer closest to the skull.

anatomy.carina.overview: A ridge at the base of the trachea, also called the tracheal carina.
anatomy.carina.function: Separates the openings of the right and left main bronchi.

anatomy.pancreatic-ducts.overview: Part of a system of ducts in the pancreas.
anatomy.pancreatic-ducts.function: Pancreatic juices containing enzymes are released into these ducts and flow into the small intestine.

anatomy.hepatic-arteries.overview: The hepatic artery is the major blood vessel that carries blood to the liver. The supplied parts include its common, proper, left and right portions.

anatomy.pelvis.overview: The bones between the lower abdomen and upper thighs that connect the spine to the legs.
anatomy.pelvis.function: Supports upper body weight, aids balance and walking, and protects the bladder, reproductive organs, colon and rectum.

anatomy.broad-ligament.overview: The layer of tissue connecting the sides of the uterus to the walls and floor of the pelvis.
anatomy.broad-ligament.function: Covers the uterus, ovaries and Fallopian tubes, and carries nerves and blood vessels to these organs.

anatomy.uterus-fundus.overview: The top part of the uterus, across from the cervix.
anatomy.uterus-fundus.function: The part of the uterus farthest from its opening, the cervix.

anatomy.coronary.lad.overview: The left anterior descending artery (LAD), also called the anterior interventricular artery, is a branch of the left coronary artery. The supplied parts include its diagonal branches.
anatomy.coronary.lad.function: Follows the groove between the ventricles on the front of the heart towards its apex, supplying heart muscle.

anatomy.coronary.circumflex.overview: The circumflex branch of the left coronary artery and its left marginal branch. In about 20-25% of people the circumflex also contributes to the posterior interventricular artery.
anatomy.coronary.circumflex.function: Follows the groove between the atria and ventricles to the left border and back of the heart; its left marginal branch follows the left border.

anatomy.coronary.right-branches.overview: Branches of the right coronary artery: the right marginal artery and, in 80-85% of people, the posterior interventricular (posterior descending) artery.
anatomy.coronary.right-branches.function: The right marginal artery runs along the right and lower border of the heart towards the apex; the posterior interventricular artery follows the groove on the back of the heart.

anatomy.extraocular-muscles.overview: Six muscles around each eye that move the eyeball: the superior, inferior, medial and lateral rectus muscles and the superior and inferior oblique muscles. They lie in the orbit but are separate from the eyeball.
anatomy.extraocular-muscles.function: The medial rectus turns the eye inward and the lateral rectus outward; the superior rectus mainly raises it and the inferior rectus mainly lowers it. The obliques also raise, lower and rotate the eye.

anatomy.levator-palpebrae.overview: The levator palpebrae superioris, a muscle in each orbit attached to the upper eyelid.
anatomy.levator-palpebrae.function: It is the only muscle that raises the upper eyelid.

anatomy.ophthalmic-vessels.overview: The ophthalmic artery, a branch of the internal carotid artery, and the superior and inferior ophthalmic veins of each eye.
anatomy.ophthalmic-vessels.function: The ophthalmic artery is the main arterial supply of the eyeball; the ophthalmic veins drain it into the cavernous sinus.

anatomy.central-retinal-vessels.overview: The central retinal artery and vein of each eye. The central artery of the retina is the most important branch of the ophthalmic artery.
anatomy.central-retinal-vessels.function: The artery supplies the internal surface of the retina; its blockage quickly causes blindness.

anatomy.larynx-muscles.overview: Intrinsic muscles of the larynx: the cricothyroid, posterior and lateral cricoarytenoid, arytenoid and thyroepiglottic muscles.
anatomy.larynx-muscles.function: They control the opening between the vocal folds and the length and tension of the vocal folds. The posterior cricoarytenoids are the only muscles that open the vocal folds; the lateral cricoarytenoids are the main ones that close them.

anatomy.vocal-folds.overview: The vocalis and thyroarytenoid muscles of the vocal folds (true vocal cords). The vocal cords are two small bands of muscle within the larynx.
anatomy.vocal-folds.function: The vocal cords vibrate to produce the voice. The thyroarytenoid relaxes the vocal ligament, allowing a softer voice.

anatomy.hyoid.overview: A U-shaped bone in the front of the neck, at the base of the jaw at about the level of the third cervical vertebra.
anatomy.hyoid.function: It does not join any other bone; it is held in place by muscles and ligaments and is an attachment site for the front neck muscles.

anatomy.bronchial-cartilage.overview: Cartilage in the walls of the bronchi. In the main bronchi, cartilage rings completely encircle the airway.
anatomy.bronchial-cartilage.function: Like the C-shaped rings of the trachea, this cartilage holds the larger airways open.

anatomy.vas-deferens.overview: A coiled tube that carries sperm out of the testes. It is a thick muscular tube whose wall is mostly smooth muscle.
anatomy.vas-deferens.function: Carries sperm from the epididymis to the ejaculatory duct, which drains into the prostatic urethra.

anatomy.seminal-vesicles.overview: A pair of tubular glands that help produce semen, between the bladder and the rectum.
anatomy.seminal-vesicles.function: They produce about 70% of the volume of semen, including an alkaline fluid that helps sperm survive.

anatomy.ejaculatory-ducts.overview: Ducts formed where each vas deferens joins the duct of a seminal vesicle.
anatomy.ejaculatory-ducts.function: They drain sperm and seminal fluid into the prostatic urethra.

anatomy.urethra.overview: The tube through which urine leaves the body from the bladder. The male urethra is about 15-20 cm long and also carries semen. The prostatic urethra passes through the prostate.
anatomy.urethra.function: Empties urine from the bladder. The prostatic urethra receives the ejaculatory ducts and the ducts of the prostate.

anatomy.uterine-ligaments.overview: Ligaments that support the uterus: the round ligaments, which run from the uterus through the inguinal canal; the cardinal ligaments, from the cervix to the side walls of the pelvis; and the uterosacral ligaments, from the cervix to the sacrum.
anatomy.uterine-ligaments.function: They support the uterus. The round ligaments help keep it tilted forward, and the cardinal ligaments carry the uterine artery and vein.

anatomy.ovarian-ligaments.overview: The two ligaments of each ovary: the suspensory ligament, a fold of peritoneum running to the pelvic wall, and the ligament of the ovary, which runs to the fundus of the uterus.
anatomy.ovarian-ligaments.function: They support the ovaries. The suspensory ligament carries the ovary's blood vessels and nerves.

anatomy.uterine-vessels.overview: The uterine arteries, branches of the internal iliac arteries, and the uterine veins.
anatomy.uterine-vessels.function: The uterine arteries supply the uterus; a venous plexus in the broad ligament drains into the uterine veins. Each uterine artery crosses above a ureter near the cervix.

anatomy.hepatic-ducts.overview: The right and left hepatic ducts, which lead bile out of the liver, and the common hepatic duct they form when they join outside the liver.
anatomy.hepatic-ducts.function: Carry bile from the liver. The common hepatic duct is joined by the cystic duct to form the common bile duct.

anatomy.hepatic-veins.overview: The left, middle and right hepatic veins.
anatomy.hepatic-veins.function: Drain blood from the liver into the inferior vena cava. Blood from the spleen, pancreas, gallbladder and gut reaches them only after passing through the liver.

anatomy.splenic-vessels.overview: The splenic artery, a branch of the celiac trunk that runs along the top of the pancreas to the spleen, and the splenic vein.
anatomy.splenic-vessels.function: The splenic artery supplies the spleen and gives branches to the stomach and pancreas. The splenic vein joins the superior mesenteric vein to form the hepatic portal vein.

anatomy.mesenteric-veins.overview: The superior and inferior mesenteric veins and the inferior pancreaticoduodenal vein, part of the portal venous system.
anatomy.mesenteric-veins.function: The portal venous system carries blood from the gut to the liver for processing. The superior mesenteric vein joins the splenic vein to form the portal vein.

anatomy.colic-vessels.overview: Arteries and veins of the colon: the ileocolic, right, middle and left colic, and sigmoid vessels, and the marginal artery (of Drummond).
anatomy.colic-vessels.function: The ileocolic, right and middle colic arteries (from the superior mesenteric artery) and the left colic and sigmoid arteries (from the inferior mesenteric artery) supply the colon. The marginal artery joins them in a continuous arterial circle along the inner border of the colon.

anatomy.rectal-vessels.overview: The superior rectal artery, the continuation of the inferior mesenteric artery, and the superior, middle and inferior rectal veins.
anatomy.rectal-vessels.function: The superior rectal artery supplies the rectum. The superior rectal vein drains into the portal venous system; the middle and inferior rectal veins drain into the systemic veins.

anatomy.cystic-vessels.overview: The cystic artery, a branch of the right hepatic artery, and the cystic vein.
anatomy.cystic-vessels.function: The cystic artery supplies the gallbladder. Cystic veins drain the neck of the gallbladder directly into the portal vein.

anatomy.iliac-veins.overview: The common, external and internal iliac veins of the pelvis, with the median sacral and internal pudendal veins. Each common iliac vein is formed by the external and internal iliac veins.
anatomy.iliac-veins.function: The external iliac vein continues from the femoral vein and drains the leg; the internal iliac vein drains most of the pelvis. The two common iliac veins join to form the inferior vena cava.

anatomy.brachiocephalic-veins.overview: The left and right brachiocephalic veins in the upper chest.
anatomy.brachiocephalic-veins.function: They drain the head, neck and arms, and join to form the superior vena cava.

anatomy.patellar-ligament.overview: The patellar ligament (often called the patellar tendon), the continuation of the quadriceps tendon below the kneecap.
anatomy.patellar-ligament.function: Connects the bottom of the kneecap to the tibial tuberosity on the front of the tibia. The kneecap above it increases the leverage of the quadriceps tendon when the leg straightens.

anatomy.stomach.overview: An organ of the digestive system in the upper left quadrant of the abdomen. It receives food from the esophagus.
anatomy.stomach.function: Helps digest food by mixing it with digestive juices and churning it into a thin liquid. Relaxing the pyloric sphincter lets this pass into the small intestine.

anatomy.esophagus.overview: The muscular tube through which food passes from the throat to the stomach. It lies behind the trachea and in front of the vertebral column.
anatomy.esophagus.function: Carries food to the stomach. It passes through an opening in the diaphragm, the esophageal hiatus, and sphincters at each end control food moving in and out.

anatomy.diaphragm.overview: The thin, dome-shaped muscle below the lungs and heart that separates the chest from the abdomen. It has three openings for structures passing between them.
anatomy.diaphragm.function: When it contracts during breathing in, the chest cavity gets larger and air flows into the lungs; when it relaxes, air flows out.

anatomy.spinal-cord.overview: A column of nerve tissue that runs from the base of the skull down the center of the back, inside the vertebral column.
anatomy.spinal-cord.function: With the brain it forms the central nervous system, carrying signals between the brain and the rest of the body.

anatomy.pituitary.overview: A pea-sized gland attached to the hypothalamus at the base of the brain. It rests in a hollow of the sphenoid bone and has anterior and posterior lobes.
anatomy.pituitary.function: Signalled by the hypothalamus, it makes hormones that control other glands and many body functions, including growth and fertility. Its hormones include growth hormone, thyroid-stimulating hormone and the hormone that stimulates the adrenal cortex.

anatomy.tongue.overview: An organ of the mouth whose surface is covered with papillae that provide friction and contain the taste buds.
anatomy.tongue.function: Moves food in the mouth, pushes it into the pharynx for swallowing, and is used in speech.

anatomy.skull.overview: The bones of the head: cranial bones that surround and protect the brain, and facial bones. The skull has 28 bones, including the auditory ossicles.
anatomy.skull.function: Protects the brain and forms the face.

anatomy.vertebral-column.overview: The spine's column of bones: usually 7 cervical, 12 thoracic and 5 lumbar vertebrae (the female body shown here has six lumbar vertebrae), the sacrum and the coccyx, reaching from the base of the skull to the tailbone.
anatomy.vertebral-column.function: Encloses the spinal cord and the fluid around it.

anatomy.adrenal-glands.overview: A pair of small, triangle-shaped glands, one on top of each kidney. Each has an outer cortex and an inner medulla.
anatomy.adrenal-glands.function: The cortex makes steroid hormones, including aldosterone and cortisol; the medulla makes epinephrine and norepinephrine, especially in stressful situations.

anatomy.testes.overview: Two egg-shaped glands inside the scrotum, also called testicles. Each is about 5 cm long.
anatomy.testes.function: Produce sperm and male hormones. Their position outside the abdomen keeps them about 3 °C cooler than the body, which sperm production needs.

anatomy.epididymis.overview: A narrow, tightly coiled tube, about 6 metres long, attached along the top and back of each testicle.
anatomy.epididymis.function: Sperm leaving the testes mature here and are stored in its lower part, then pass into the vas deferens.

anatomy.penis.overview: An external male reproductive organ made of three columns of erectile tissue: two corpora cavernosa and the corpus spongiosum, which surrounds the urethra and widens into the glans.
anatomy.penis.function: Contains the urethra, which carries semen and urine out of the body.

anatomy.sternum.overview: The breastbone: the long flat bone that forms the center front of the chest wall.
anatomy.sternum.function: The collarbones and the first seven ribs attach to it.

anatomy.ribs.overview: The ribs of the chest; the thoracic cage is made of the sternum and 24 ribs.
anatomy.ribs.function: The intercostal muscles between the ribs move them during breathing.

anatomy.clavicles.overview: The collarbones: a pair of bones at the base of the front of the neck.
anatomy.clavicles.function: Connect the breastbone to the shoulder blades.

anatomy.scapulae.overview: The shoulder blades: a pair of triangular bones at the back of the shoulder.
anatomy.scapulae.function: Each connects the collarbone with the upper arm bone. Muscles attached to them move the shoulder and arm.

anatomy.humerus.overview: The upper arm bone, one in each arm.
anatomy.humerus.function: The pectoralis major, deltoid and rotator cuff muscles connect to it and move the arm; muscles along it move the forearm.

anatomy.forearm-bones.overview: The radius and ulna, the two parallel bones of each forearm; the radius lies on the outer (lateral) side and the ulna on the inner (medial) side.
anatomy.forearm-bones.function: The 20 or more muscles that move the wrist, hand and fingers lie along the forearm.

anatomy.hand-bones.overview: The bones of the hands: 16 carpals, 10 metacarpals and 28 phalanges in the two hands.
anatomy.hand-bones.function: Part of the upper extremity of the appendicular skeleton.

anatomy.foot-bones.overview: The bones of the feet: 14 tarsals, 10 metatarsals and 28 phalanges in the two feet.
anatomy.foot-bones.function: Part of the lower extremity of the appendicular skeleton.

anatomy.sacrum.overview: The large, triangle-shaped bone in the lower spine, made of 5 fused bones of the spine.

anatomy.mandible.overview: The lower jaw: the largest and strongest bone in the face, forming part of the mouth.
anatomy.mandible.function: The only movable bone of the skull. It holds the bottom teeth, and the chewing muscles connect to it.

anatomy.maxillae.overview: The bones that form the upper jaw, the roof of the mouth, and parts of the eye socket and nose.
anatomy.maxillae.function: Hold the top teeth in place.

anatomy.teeth.overview: The teeth of the source model. A complete permanent set has 32 teeth; a set of primary teeth has 20.
anatomy.teeth.function: The shape of each tooth type corresponds to the way it handles food.

anatomy.soft-palate.overview: The back, muscular part of the roof of the mouth, ending in a small flap called the uvula.
anatomy.soft-palate.function: During swallowing the soft palate and uvula move upward to keep food out of the nasal cavity.

anatomy.pharynx-muscles.overview: The constrictor muscles of the pharynx, the hollow, muscular tube in the neck that runs from behind the nose to the larynx and esophagus.
anatomy.pharynx-muscles.function: When food reaches the pharynx, an involuntary swallowing reflex and wave-like muscle movements push it into the esophagus.

anatomy.salivary-glands.overview: The submandibular and sublingual glands, two of the three pairs of major salivary glands. The parotid glands, the third pair, have their own study card.
anatomy.salivary-glands.function: Salivary glands make saliva and empty it into the mouth through ducts.

anatomy.nasal-bones.overview: Two small bones that, with extensions of the maxillae, form the bony bridge of the nose.
anatomy.nasal-bones.function: The rest of the nose's framework is flexible cartilage.

anatomy.carotid-arteries.overview: Major arteries, one on each side of the neck. The left common carotid artery branches from the aortic arch and the right from the brachiocephalic trunk; each divides at about the level of C4 into the internal and external carotid arteries.
anatomy.carotid-arteries.function: Carry blood from the heart to the head. With the vertebral arteries, the internal carotid arteries supply the brain.

anatomy.subclavian-arteries.overview: The left and right subclavian arteries. The left subclavian artery branches from the aortic arch and the right from the brachiocephalic trunk.

anatomy.leg-arteries.overview: The external iliac arteries, whose branches supply the legs.
anatomy.leg-arteries.function: Branches of the external iliac artery supply the legs.

anatomy.intercostal-muscles.overview: Muscles in the spaces between the ribs.
anatomy.intercostal-muscles.function: Move the ribs in breathing: the external intercostals raise the ribs when breathing in.

anatomy.pectoralis-major.overview: The most superficial muscle of the chest on each side, one of the muscles that connect to the humerus. It arises from the clavicle, the sternum and the upper six costal cartilages.
anatomy.pectoralis-major.function: Adducts and medially rotates the arm; its clavicular part also flexes it.

anatomy.deltoids.overview: The deltoid muscle on each side; the source model divides it into three parts.
anatomy.deltoids.function: Connects to the humerus and moves the arm.

anatomy.biceps-brachii.overview: The biceps brachii of each arm, with its long and short heads.
anatomy.biceps-brachii.function: One of the muscles along the humerus that move the forearm.

anatomy.triceps-brachii.overview: The triceps brachii of each arm, with its long, lateral and medial heads.
anatomy.triceps-brachii.function: One of the muscles along the humerus that move the forearm.

anatomy.trapezius.overview: A broad, flat, triangular muscle on each side, the most superficial of the back muscles. It runs from the skull and the spinous processes of C7-T12 to the clavicle and the scapula.
anatomy.trapezius.function: Moves the scapula: the upper fibres raise it and rotate it as the arm is lifted, the middle fibres pull it back and the lower fibres pull it down.

anatomy.gluteus-maximus.overview: One of the gluteal muscles on each side, the posterior group of the muscles that move the thigh.
anatomy.gluteus-maximus.function: The gluteal muscles are the largest muscle mass among the muscles that move the thigh.

anatomy.quadriceps.overview: The quadriceps femoris group of each thigh: the rectus femoris and three vastus muscles. The female and male bodies show the rectus femoris only.
anatomy.quadriceps.function: Straightens the leg at the knee.

anatomy.hamstrings.overview: The hamstring muscles of each thigh: the biceps femoris, semitendinosus and semimembranosus.
anatomy.hamstrings.function: Bend the leg at the knee, working against the quadriceps.

anatomy.calf-muscles.overview: The gastrocnemius and soleus muscles of each lower leg.
anatomy.calf-muscles.function: Point the foot downward (plantar flexion), working against the tibialis anterior.

anatomy.tibialis-anterior.overview: A muscle of each lower leg.
anatomy.tibialis-anterior.function: Lifts the foot upward (dorsiflexion), working against the calf muscles.

anatomy.intervertebral-disks.overview: Soft disks filled with a jelly-like substance between the vertebrae.
anatomy.intervertebral-disks.function: Cushion the vertebrae and keep them in place. As the disks age they break down and lose their cushioning.

anatomy.breasts.overview: The breasts (mammary glands): glandular organs on the chest made of connective tissue, fat, and breast tissue containing the glands that can make milk.
anatomy.breasts.function: Their glands can make milk, which can flow out through the nipple, the small raised area in the center of each breast. The areola is the darker skin surrounding the nipple.

anatomy.tonsils.overview: The palatine tonsils: two small masses of lymphoid tissue on either side of the throat, near where the mouth opens into the pharynx.
anatomy.tonsils.function: Lymphocytes and macrophages in the tonsils help protect against harmful substances and germs entering through the nose or mouth. The pharyngeal tonsils (adenoids) and lingual tonsils are not supplied here.

anatomy.thyroid.overview: A very vascular gland in the neck, beneath the larynx. Its two lobes lie on each side of the trachea and are joined by a narrow band called the isthmus.
anatomy.thyroid.function: Makes thyroid hormones, which contain iodine and help regulate growth and metabolism, and the hormone calcitonin.

anatomy.parathyroid-glands.overview: Four pea-sized glands on the surface of the thyroid, in the neck.
anatomy.parathyroid-glands.function: Their only purpose is to make parathyroid hormone, which raises the calcium level in the blood and keeps the body's calcium in balance.

anatomy.parotid-glands.overview: The largest of the salivary glands. There are two parotid glands, one in front of and just below each ear.
anatomy.parotid-glands.function: Like the other salivary glands, they make saliva and release it into the mouth. Most salivary gland tumors begin in the parotid glands.

anatomy.scrotum.overview: In males, the external sac that contains the testicles.
anatomy.scrotum.function: Holds the testes outside the abdomen, which keeps them about 3 °C cooler than the body, as sperm production needs.

anatomy.vulva.overview: The external female genital organs. The vulva includes the inner and outer lips of the vagina, the clitoris, the opening of the vagina and its glands, the opening of the urethra, and the mons pubis, the rounded area in front of the pubic bones.
anatomy.vulva.function: Surrounds the openings of the vagina and the urethra. The Bartholin glands lie on each side of the vaginal opening.

not_modelled.note: No open anatomical source supplies a model of this structure, so no body shows it. Locate selects the nearest supplied structure when the current body has one.

anatomy.adenoids.overview: A patch of lymphatic tissue high up in the throat, just behind the nose, near the opening of the nasal cavity into the pharynx. They are also called the pharyngeal tonsils.
anatomy.adenoids.function: With the other tonsils, they trap germs coming in through the mouth and nose. They usually start to shrink after about age 5 and are almost completely gone by the teenage years.

anatomy.lingual-tonsils.overview: Tonsils on the back surface of the tongue, near the opening of the mouth into the pharynx.
anatomy.lingual-tonsils.function: Like the other tonsils, their lymphocytes and macrophages help protect against harmful substances and germs entering through the nose or mouth.

not_modelled.title: Lingual tonsils
not_modelled.note: No open anatomical source supplies a model of this structure, so no body shows it. Locate selects the nearest supplied structure when the current body has one.

anatomy.gluteus-medius.overview: A fan-shaped gluteal muscle on each side, lying between the gluteus maximus and the gluteus minimus. It runs from the outer surface of the ilium to the greater trochanter of the femur.
anatomy.gluteus-medius.function: Moves the thigh away from the body's midline (abduction) and rotates it inward. It steadies the pelvis when walking, keeping the opposite side from dropping.

anatomy.gluteus-minimus.overview: The deepest and smallest of the three gluteal muscles on each side. It runs from the ilium to the front of the greater trochanter of the femur.
anatomy.gluteus-minimus.function: Like the gluteus medius, it moves the thigh away from the midline, rotates it inward and steadies the pelvis when walking.

anatomy.iliopsoas.overview: An anterior muscle of the hip on each side, made of two muscles: the psoas major, which arises from the lumbar vertebrae, and the iliacus, which arises from the iliac fossa of the pelvis. They insert together onto the lesser trochanter of the femur.
anatomy.iliopsoas.function: Flexes the thigh, bending the hip.

anatomy.deep-back-muscles.overview: The deep (intrinsic) back muscles on each side of the vertebral column. They include the erector spinae group, a large muscle mass extending from the sacrum to the skull, and the deeper muscles between the spinous and transverse processes of the vertebrae.
anatomy.deep-back-muscles.function: Extend the vertebral column to maintain erect posture, and help bend and turn the spine.

anatomy.muscles-of-mastication.overview: The four pairs of chewing muscles: the masseter, the temporalis and the medial and lateral pterygoids. All of them connect to the mandible, and they are some of the strongest muscles in the body.
anatomy.muscles-of-mastication.function: The masseter, temporalis and medial pterygoid raise the mandible, closing the mouth; the temporalis also pulls the jaw back. The lateral pterygoids push the jaw forward and move it from side to side.

anatomy.scalenes.overview: Three paired muscles on the side of the neck: the anterior, middle and posterior scalenes. They run from the transverse processes of the cervical vertebrae to the first rib (anterior and middle scalenes) and the second rib (posterior scalene).
anatomy.scalenes.function: They raise the first and second ribs, acting as accessory muscles of breathing, and bend the neck forward and to the side.

anatomy.rectus-abdominis.overview: A long muscle on each side of the front of the abdominal wall. It runs from the crest of the pubis to the xiphoid process of the sternum and the costal cartilages of ribs 5-7.
anatomy.rectus-abdominis.function: Helps the flat abdominal muscles compress the abdominal organs, steadies the pelvis when walking and pulls the ribs down.

anatomy.abdominal-obliques.overview: The external and internal oblique muscles on each side, two of the layered muscle pairs of the abdominal wall. The external oblique, the largest and most superficial, runs from ribs 5-12 to the iliac crest and pubic tubercle; the internal oblique lies deep to it.
anatomy.abdominal-obliques.function: Both rotate the torso. The internal obliques, contracting together, also compress the abdomen.

anatomy.quadratus-lumborum.overview: A thick, four-sided muscle on each side of the posterior abdominal wall, behind the psoas major. It runs from the iliac crest to the lowest rib and the transverse processes of the L1-L4 vertebrae.
anatomy.quadratus-lumborum.function: Extends the vertebral column and bends it to the side. It also holds the 12th rib steady when breathing in, so that the diaphragm contracts more efficiently.

anatomy.latissimus-dorsi.overview: A broad muscle of the lower back on each side. It arises from the spinous processes of T6-T12, the thoracolumbar fascia, the iliac crest and the lowest three ribs, and its fibres converge into a tendon attached to the humerus.
anatomy.latissimus-dorsi.function: Extends, adducts and medially rotates the arm.

anatomy.serratus-anterior.overview: A muscle on each side of the chest wall, made of strips that arise from the outer surfaces of ribs 1-8 and attach to the medial border of the scapula.
anatomy.serratus-anterior.function: Rotates the scapula so the arm can be raised above shoulder height, and holds the scapula against the ribcage.

anatomy.sternocleidomastoid.overview: A superficial muscle on each side of the neck with two heads: the sternal head from the manubrium of the sternum and the clavicular head from the medial third of the clavicle. It runs up to the mastoid process of the temporal bone, and its borders outline the anterior and posterior triangles of the neck.
anatomy.sternocleidomastoid.function: Acting on one side, it bends the neck to that side and rotates it; acting together, the two muscles extend the head at the joints between the skull and the atlas. It is supplied by the accessory nerve.

anatomy.levator-scapulae.overview: A muscle at the back and side of the neck, one on each side. It runs from the transverse processes of the first four cervical vertebrae (C1-C4) to the medial border of the scapula.
anatomy.levator-scapulae.function: Raises the scapula. It is supplied by the dorsal scapular nerve.

anatomy.infrahyoid-muscles.overview: The muscles below the hyoid bone at the front of the neck: the sternohyoid, omohyoid, sternothyroid and thyrohyoid. The sternothyroid runs from the manubrium of the sternum to the thyroid cartilage, and the thyrohyoid from the thyroid cartilage to the hyoid. The female and male bodies show the sternothyroid and thyrohyoid only.
anatomy.infrahyoid-muscles.function: They pull the hyoid bone down, and the sternothyroid pulls the thyroid cartilage down; when the hyoid is held still, the thyrohyoid raises the larynx. They are supplied by the upper cervical nerves (C1-C3).

anatomy.prevertebral-muscles.overview: Muscles on the front of the cervical spine, one group on each side: the longus colli and longus capitis, with the small rectus capitis anterior and lateralis below the skull. The longus colli runs between the vertebral bodies and transverse processes from the upper thoracic vertebrae to the atlas; the longus capitis runs from the cervical transverse processes to the base of the skull.
anatomy.prevertebral-muscles.function: They flex the neck and the head and help to steady the cervical spine. They are supplied by the anterior rami of the cervical spinal nerves.

anatomy.digastric.overview: A small muscle below the jaw, one on each side, with two bellies joined by a tendon that a fibrous sling holds to the hyoid bone. The anterior belly attaches to the mandible and the posterior belly to the mastoid process of the skull.
anatomy.digastric.function: Lowers the mandible, opening the mouth, and raises the hyoid bone. The two bellies have different nerves: a branch of the mandibular nerve for the anterior belly and the facial nerve for the posterior belly.

anatomy.internal-jugular-veins.overview: A large vein on each side of the neck. It begins at the base of the skull, continuing the sigmoid sinus, leaves the skull through the jugular foramen and runs down the neck in the carotid sheath, beside the common carotid artery and deep to the sternocleidomastoid.
anatomy.internal-jugular-veins.function: Carries blood from inside the skull and, through tributaries such as the facial, lingual and thyroid veins, from the face and neck. Behind the sternal end of the clavicle it joins the subclavian vein to form the brachiocephalic vein.

anatomy.cerebral-hemispheres.overview: The two halves of the cerebrum, the largest part of the brain, divided by a deep longitudinal fissure and joined by the corpus callosum. Each has frontal, parietal, temporal and occipital lobes, and a fifth lobe, the insula, deep inside.
anatomy.cerebral-hemispheres.function: The association areas of the lobes handle higher functions: the frontal lobe intellect, personality, mood and language; the parietal lobe language, calculation and visuospatial functions; the temporal lobe memory, language and hearing; and the occipital lobe vision.

anatomy.motor-cortex.overview: The precentral gyrus: the ridge just in front of the central sulcus, at the back of each frontal lobe. It is the location of the primary motor cortex.
anatomy.motor-cortex.function: The corticospinal and corticobulbar tracts, which give voluntary control of the muscles of the body and face, begin in the primary motor cortex and nearby areas of the cortex.

anatomy.sensory-cortex.overview: The postcentral gyrus: the ridge just behind the central sulcus, at the front of each parietal lobe. It is the location of the primary somatosensory cortex.
anatomy.sensory-cortex.function: Receives the sensory pathways that carry touch, pressure, vibration and the sense of body position (proprioception) up from the body through the spinal cord and the thalamus.

anatomy.auditory-cortex.overview: The superior temporal gyrus, the ridge below the lateral sulcus at the top of each temporal lobe, with the transverse temporal (Heschl's) gyrus. The temporal lobe holds the primary auditory cortex.

anatomy.basal-ganglia.overview: Clusters of nerve cells deep in the brain, around the thalamus. The source models include the caudate nucleus, putamen, globus pallidus and nucleus accumbens, and the HRA bodies also the subthalamic nucleus; the substantia nigra has its own card.
anatomy.basal-ganglia.function: Part of the circuits that control movement. The putamen mainly receives input from the motor and sensory areas of the cortex and projects back to the motor areas, and the subthalamic nucleus acts as a brake that keeps unwanted movements from starting.

anatomy.substantia-nigra.overview: A pigmented nucleus in the midbrain, one on each side, between the two parts of each cerebral peduncle. It looks dark in brain specimens because of the pigment neuromelanin in its cells.
anatomy.substantia-nigra.function: Part of the basal ganglia circuits that control movement: its compact part (pars compacta) is one of their intrinsic nuclei and its reticular part (pars reticulata) one of their output nuclei.

anatomy.patella.overview: The kneecap: a triangular bone at the front of the knee, set within the quadriceps tendon. It is the largest sesamoid bone in the body.
anatomy.patella.function: Increases the leverage of the quadriceps tendon, making the muscle more efficient at straightening the leg, and protects the front of the knee joint.

anatomy.fibula.overview: The thinner bone on the outer side of the lower leg, beside the tibia. Its lower end, the lateral malleolus, forms the bony bump on the outside of the ankle.
anatomy.fibula.function: Serves mainly as an attachment for muscles rather than bearing weight. It joins the tibia just below the knee and the talus at the ankle, and the lateral collateral ligament of the knee attaches to its head.

anatomy.coccyx.overview: The tailbone: the small bone at the bottom of the spine, below the sacrum, made of three to five fused vertebrae.
anatomy.coccyx.function: The last part of the vertebral column. It joins the tip of the sacrum and, unlike the vertebrae above it, has no canal for the spinal cord.

anatomy.cervical-vertebrae.overview: The seven vertebrae of the neck, C1 to C7. The first two, C1 and C2 (the atlas and axis), are specialized to allow the head to move.
anatomy.cervical-vertebrae.function: Support the head and let the neck move. Their openings line up with those of the other vertebrae to form the vertebral canal, which encloses the spinal cord.

anatomy.thoracic-vertebrae.overview: The twelve vertebrae of the upper and middle back, T1 to T12, recognized by their joints with the ribs.
anatomy.thoracic-vertebrae.function: Together with the ribs and sternum they form the bony thorax.

anatomy.lumbar-vertebrae.overview: The vertebrae of the lower back, the largest in the vertebral column, with large kidney-shaped bodies. There are usually five; the female body shown here has six.
anatomy.lumbar-vertebrae.function: Built to support the weight of the torso.

anatomy.fovea.overview: A small depression in the center of the macula, at the back of each eye.
anatomy.fovea.function: Has a high concentration of light-detecting cells. The macula around it controls sharp, straight-ahead vision.

anatomy.optic-disc.overview: The place at the back of each eye where the optic nerve meets the retina.
anatomy.optic-disc.function: Contains no light-detecting cells. Swelling of the optic disc can be a sign of raised pressure inside the skull.

anatomy.aqueous-humor.overview: A clear, plasma-like fluid that fills the chambers at the front of each eye.
anatomy.aqueous-humor.function: Nourishes and protects the eye. It is produced constantly, with the help of the ciliary body, and drains away through the trabecular meshwork.

anatomy.eye-drainage.overview: The trabecular meshwork, an area of tissue at the base of the cornea near the front chamber of the eye, with the nearby Schlemm's canal.
anatomy.eye-drainage.function: Aqueous humor drains out of the eye through the trabecular meshwork. If its drainage is blocked, glaucoma can result.

anatomy.prostate-zones.overview: The prostate's zones by tissue type: the peripheral zone, the main body of the gland at the back (about 65% of it); the central zone around the ejaculatory ducts (about 25%); and the transition zone around the urethra (5-10%).
anatomy.prostate-zones.function: The glands of the transition zone are the ones that typically enlarge in benign prostatic hyperplasia, which can squeeze the urethra.

anatomy.bladder-trigone.overview: A smooth-walled triangular area inside the base (fundus) of the bladder, marked out by the openings of the two ureters and of the urethra.
anatomy.bladder-trigone.function: Urine enters the bladder through the ureters, whose openings mark two of its corners, and leaves through the urethra at the third.

anatomy.colon-segments.overview: The parts of the colon: the ascending colon rises from the cecum on the right, turns at the hepatic flexure into the transverse colon, which runs across to the spleen, and turns down at the splenic flexure into the descending colon, which becomes the sigmoid colon.
anatomy.colon-segments.function: Together they make up most of the colon, which absorbs water and moves waste toward the rectum.

anatomy.heart.papillary-muscles.overview: Muscles on the inner walls of the ventricles, five in total, joined by fibrous cords (chordae tendineae) to the cusps of the mitral and tricuspid valves.
anatomy.heart.papillary-muscles.function: They contract as the ventricles pump, keeping the valve leaflets from being pushed back into the atria.

anatomy.ear.overview: The organ of hearing. Sound waves have to reach the inner ear, which connects to the brain through the auditory nerve; the eardrum and the middle ear lie on the way.
anatomy.ear.function: Hearing. Damage to the inner ear or the auditory nerve, or anything that keeps sound waves from reaching the inner ear, such as earwax, fluid or a punctured eardrum, can cause hearing loss.

not_modelled.title: Ears
not_modelled.note: No open anatomical source supplies a model of this structure, so no body shows it. Locate selects the nearest supplied structure when the current body has one.

anatomy.sinuses.overview: Hollow air spaces within the bones surrounding the nose.
anatomy.sinuses.function: They produce mucus, which drains into the nose. If the nose is swollen, this can block the sinuses and cause pain.

not_modelled.title: Sinuses
not_modelled.note: No open anatomical source supplies a model of this structure, so no body shows it. Locate selects the nearest supplied structure when the current body has one.

anatomy.venae-cavae.overview: The two venae cavae, the large veins through which blood returns to the heart: the superior vena cava and the inferior vena cava.
anatomy.venae-cavae.function: Return oxygen-poor blood from the body to the right atrium.

heart-lung.title: Heart ↔ lungs
heart-lung.scope: A conceptual sequence with explicit source selections. Mesh shape and proximity do not establish flow or vessel continuity. No flow simulation or internal channel is drawn.

vena-cava.title: Vena cava
vena-cava.text: Blood returns from the body toward the right atrium.

right-atrium.title: Right atrium
right-atrium.text: The right atrium receives this returning blood.

tricuspid.title: Tricuspid valve
tricuspid.text: Blood passes toward the right ventricle through this valve.

right-ventricle.title: Right ventricle
right-ventricle.text: The right ventricle pumps blood toward the lungs.

pulmonary-valve.title: Pulmonary valve
pulmonary-valve.text: This valve lies on the way to the pulmonary artery.

pulmonary-trunk.title: Toward either lung
pulmonary-trunk.text: Follow a pulmonary arterial branch toward either lung.

left-artery.title: Left pulmonary artery
left-artery.text: The pulmonary arteries carry oxygen-poor blood toward the lungs.

right-artery.title: Right pulmonary artery
right-artery.text: The pulmonary arteries carry oxygen-poor blood toward the lungs.

left-exchange.title: Left lung: gas exchange
left-exchange.text: Oxygen enters blood across the alveoli; carbon dioxide moves into the air spaces.
left-exchange.gap: Lung surface shown for context. Individual alveoli and the capillary network are not supplied by this atlas.

right-exchange.title: Right lung: gas exchange
right-exchange.text: Oxygen enters blood across the alveoli; carbon dioxide moves into the air spaces.
right-exchange.gap: Lung surface shown for context. Individual alveoli and the capillary network are not supplied by this atlas.

pulmonary-veins.title: Pulmonary veins
pulmonary-veins.text: Oxygen-rich blood returns from the lungs through these veins.

left-atrium.title: Left atrium
left-atrium.text: Blood returning from the lungs enters the left atrium.

mitral.title: Mitral valve
mitral.text: Blood passes through this valve toward the left ventricle.

left-ventricle.title: Left ventricle
left-ventricle.text: The left ventricle pumps blood toward the body.

aortic-valve.title: Aortic valve
aortic-valve.text: This valve lies between the left ventricle and aorta.

aorta.title: Aorta
aorta.text: Blood leaves the heart through the aorta.

systemic-gap.title: Through the body and back
systemic-gap.text: Blood circulates through the body before returning to the heart.
systemic-gap.gap: Whole-body context only. A complete systemic vessel and tissue-capillary route is not mapped here.

condition.aortic-stenosis.title: Aortic stenosis
condition.aortic-stenosis.summary: The aortic valve opening is too small or narrow, for example when the valve forms with two flaps instead of three. Valve problems can make the heart work harder and affect its ability to pump blood.
condition.aortic-stenosis.location: The aortic valve is at the outlet from the left ventricle into the aorta.
condition.aortic-stenosis.not_depicted: Pathological narrowing, leakage, leaflet motion and blood flow are not depicted.

condition.mitral-regurgitation.title: Mitral regurgitation
condition.mitral-regurgitation.summary: An incompletely closed mitral valve can allow blood to pass backward.
condition.mitral-regurgitation.location: The mitral valve connects the left atrium and left ventricle.
condition.mitral-regurgitation.not_depicted: Pathological narrowing, leakage, leaflet motion and blood flow are not depicted.

condition.coronary-heart-disease.title: Coronary heart disease
condition.coronary-heart-disease.summary: Plaque made of cholesterol and other substances builds up in the coronary arteries, narrowing them and reducing blood flow to the heart muscle.
condition.coronary-heart-disease.location: The right and left coronary arteries branch from the aorta and run over the surface of the heart.
condition.coronary-heart-disease.not_depicted: Plaque, arterial narrowing and blood flow are not depicted.

condition.aortic-aneurysm.title: Aortic aneurysm
condition.aortic-aneurysm.summary: A balloon-like bulge in the wall of the aorta. A large aneurysm can burst or tear the artery wall, which can be life-threatening.
condition.aortic-aneurysm.location: The aorta leaves the left ventricle and carries oxygen-rich blood to the body.
condition.aortic-aneurysm.not_depicted: The bulge, any tear and blood flow are not depicted.

condition.pulmonary-embolism.title: Pulmonary embolism
condition.pulmonary-embolism.summary: A blood clot, usually from a deep vein in the leg, breaks loose and travels through the bloodstream to the lungs.
condition.pulmonary-embolism.location: Clots reach the lungs through the pulmonary arteries, which carry blood from the right ventricle to both lungs.
condition.pulmonary-embolism.not_depicted: Clots, blocked vessels and blood flow are not depicted.

condition.copd.title: Chronic obstructive pulmonary disease (COPD)
condition.copd.summary: A long-term lung disease that blocks airflow and makes it hard to breathe. It mainly includes emphysema, damage to the walls between air sacs, and chronic bronchitis, in which thick mucus forms in the airways.
condition.copd.location: Air passes through the trachea and the branching bronchi to the tiny air sacs of both lungs.
condition.copd.not_depicted: Damaged air sacs, mucus and airflow are not depicted.

condition.asthma.title: Asthma
condition.asthma.summary: A long-term condition in which the airways in the lungs can become inflamed and narrowed, making it harder for air to flow out.
condition.asthma.location: The bronchi branch into smaller and smaller airways inside both lungs.
condition.asthma.not_depicted: Airway inflammation, narrowing and airflow are not depicted.

condition.gallstones.title: Gallstones
condition.gallstones.summary: Hard, pebble-like pieces of material, usually made of cholesterol or bilirubin, that develop in the gallbladder. Stones that block the bile ducts can cause sudden pain that needs prompt medical attention.
condition.gallstones.location: The gallbladder stores bile and squeezes it through the bile ducts into the small intestine.
condition.gallstones.not_depicted: Stones, blocked ducts and bile flow are not depicted.

condition.cirrhosis.title: Cirrhosis
condition.cirrhosis.summary: Scar tissue replaces healthy liver tissue, permanently damaging the liver and preventing it from working normally.
condition.cirrhosis.location: The liver lies mainly in the upper right abdomen, just beneath the diaphragm.
condition.cirrhosis.not_depicted: Scarring and changes in liver shape or texture are not depicted.

condition.pancreatitis.title: Pancreatitis
condition.pancreatitis.summary: Inflammation of the pancreas. Acute pancreatitis is short term; chronic pancreatitis can get worse over time. Causes include gallstones and heavy alcohol use.
condition.pancreatitis.location: The pancreas releases digestive enzymes into the small intestine and hormones into the blood.
condition.pancreatitis.not_depicted: Inflammation and tissue damage are not depicted.

condition.appendicitis.title: Appendicitis
condition.appendicitis.summary: Inflammation of the appendix, and the most common cause of sudden abdominal pain that needs surgery. Quick treatment prevents most complications.
condition.appendicitis.location: The appendix is a finger-shaped pouch attached to the cecum, the first part of the large intestine.
condition.appendicitis.not_depicted: Inflammation and swelling are not depicted.

condition.kidney-stones.title: Kidney stones
condition.kidney-stones.summary: A solid, pebble-like piece of material that can form in one or both kidneys when urine has high levels of certain minerals. A stone passing through the urinary tract can cause sharp pain in the back, side, lower abdomen or groin.
condition.kidney-stones.location: Urine flows from the kidneys through the ureters to the bladder.
condition.kidney-stones.not_depicted: Stones and urine flow are not depicted.

condition.bph.title: Enlarged prostate (benign prostatic hyperplasia)
condition.bph.summary: The prostate grows larger than normal, but not because of cancer. As it grows it can squeeze the urethra and make emptying the bladder harder.
condition.bph.location: The prostate sits below the bladder and surrounds the urethra at the neck of the bladder.
condition.bph.not_depicted: Prostate enlargement and urine flow are not depicted.

condition.endometriosis.title: Endometriosis
condition.endometriosis.summary: Tissue similar to the lining of the uterus grows outside the uterus. It can cause pain, infertility and other symptoms.
condition.endometriosis.location: The uterus is a muscular organ, with an ovary on each side of it.
condition.endometriosis.not_depicted: Tissue growing outside the uterus is not depicted.

condition.stroke.title: Stroke
condition.stroke.summary: Blood flow to part of the brain is lost, so brain cells cannot get the oxygen and nutrients they need and start to die within minutes. Most strokes are ischemic, caused by a clot blocking a blood vessel in the brain; hemorrhagic strokes are caused by a vessel that breaks and bleeds into the brain. A stroke needs emergency help right away.
condition.stroke.location: The brain is divided into the cerebrum, diencephalon, brain stem and cerebellum. A stroke affecting the cerebellum may cause dizziness, nausea and problems with balance and coordination.
condition.stroke.not_depicted: Blocked or bleeding blood vessels, blood flow and damaged brain tissue are not depicted.

condition.alzheimers.title: Alzheimer's disease
condition.alzheimers.summary: The most common form of dementia among older people. It begins slowly over many years, first involving the parts of the brain that control thought, memory and language, and its symptoms get worse over time. It is not a normal part of aging.
condition.alzheimers.location: The brain is divided into the cerebrum, diencephalon, brain stem and cerebellum.
condition.alzheimers.not_depicted: Brain changes caused by the disease are not depicted.

condition.parkinsons.title: Parkinson's disease
condition.parkinsons.summary: A movement disorder in which the brain cells that make the chemical dopamine slowly die. Without enough dopamine, movement becomes hard to control; symptoms include trembling, stiffness, slowness and poor balance, often starting on one side of the body.
condition.parkinsons.location: The brain is divided into the cerebrum, diencephalon, brain stem and cerebellum.
condition.parkinsons.not_depicted: The affected brain cells and dopamine signaling are not depicted.

condition.epilepsy.title: Epilepsy
condition.epilepsy.summary: A brain disorder that causes recurring seizures, which happen when clusters of nerve cells in the brain send out the wrong signals. Medicines can control seizures for most people.
condition.epilepsy.location: The brain is divided into the cerebrum, diencephalon, brain stem and cerebellum.
condition.epilepsy.not_depicted: Nerve-cell signaling and seizure activity are not depicted.

condition.cataracts.title: Cataracts
condition.cataracts.summary: A cloudy area in the lens of the eye. Cataracts are very common with age and can make vision blurry, hazy or less colorful. Surgery can remove them.
condition.cataracts.location: The lens is a clear inner part of the eye that works with the cornea to focus light on the retina.
condition.cataracts.not_depicted: Clouding of the lens is not depicted.

condition.glaucoma.title: Glaucoma
condition.glaucoma.summary: A group of eye diseases that can cause vision loss and blindness by damaging the optic nerve at the back of the eye. It often has no symptoms at first; early treatment can often stop the damage.
condition.glaucoma.location: Each optic nerve carries signals from the retina at the back of the eye to the brain.
condition.glaucoma.not_depicted: Optic nerve damage and vision loss are not depicted.

condition.amd.title: Age-related macular degeneration (AMD)
condition.amd.summary: Aging damages the macula, the part of the retina that controls sharp, straight-ahead vision, blurring central vision. Most people have dry AMD, in which the macula gets thinner with age.
condition.amd.location: The macula is part of the retina, the light-sensitive tissue at the back of the eye.
condition.amd.not_depicted: Thinning or other damage to the macula is not depicted.

condition.diabetic-retinopathy.title: Diabetic retinopathy
condition.diabetic-retinopathy.summary: An eye condition that can cause vision loss and blindness in people with diabetes. It affects blood vessels in the retina and may have no symptoms at first.
condition.diabetic-retinopathy.location: The retina is the light-sensitive layer of tissue at the back of the eye.
condition.diabetic-retinopathy.not_depicted: Retinal blood vessels and their damage are not depicted.

condition.acl-injury.title: Anterior cruciate ligament (ACL) injury
condition.acl-injury.summary: Over-stretching or tearing, partial or complete, of the ACL in the knee. It can happen from a hard hit to the side of the knee, over-extending the knee, or quickly stopping and changing direction while running, landing from a jump or turning. It often occurs with other injuries, such as tears of the MCL and the menisci.
condition.acl-injury.location: The ACL is in the middle of the knee, connecting the thigh bone and shin bone.
condition.acl-injury.not_depicted: The torn ligament and knee motion are not depicted.

condition.meniscus-tear.title: Meniscus tear
